also: I am deeply grateful to you

terms.gloss: thank you, for a kindness done

terms.grammar: grātiam habēre alicui, to feel gratitude; grātiās agere is to say thank you formally
evidence: Ter. Eun. 5.8.61: bene fēcistī; grātiam habeō maximam (Lewis & Short), s.v. bene
Ter. Ad. 5.9.14: omnibus grātiam habeō (Lewis & Short), s.v. sēorsus

terms.gloss: you have done me a great kindness: I’m much obliged to you
terms.grammar: pergrātum, neuter, “a very welcome thing”; what was done follows with quod and the indicative
evidence: Cic. Att. 2.4.1: fēcistī mihi pergrātum, quod Serāpiōnis librum ad mē mīsistī (Lewis & Short s.v. quod)
Traupman 105: I’m much obliged to you for sending me your book, fēcistī mihi pergrātum quod librum ad mē mīsistī
terms.comment: The letter-writer’s thanks: English thanks “for” something, Latin says what was done in a quod clause. In the future, as a request: grātum mihi fēceris sī ….

terms.grammar: grātiās agere, to give thanks, with the person in the dative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.24.2: tibi maximās grātiās agō (Lewis & Short s.v. grātia)
Traupman 17: thanks a lot!, grātiās maximās!
terms.comment: Formal thanks, as in a letter; face to face comedy says Amō tē or Grātiam habeō.

evidence: Traupman 56: multās grātiās!, thanks a lot
Traupman 173: grātiās multās!, thanks a lot
terms.comment: We have found no classical instance without agere (Lewis & Short quotes it only with the verb), but it is used so in modern Latin; the classical forms are grātiās agō and grātiam habeō. Traupman 17 also gives grātiās maximās!, thanks a lot, and sescentās grātiās!, thanks a million (sescentī, six hundred, is the comic “countless”: Plaut. Trin. 3.3.62, Lewis & Short).
